passage: Bhavna dropped by the delivery hub in Gurugram to return Kunal's charger and stopped at the loading bay. Her friend, the man who cooked for six in their shared flat and apologised to the cat, was shouting at a rider over a crushed parcel. "Three minutes late, and this? Do you want the job or not?" The rider stood with his helmet in his hands. Kunal's supervisor lanyard swung as he turned away. On the metro home Bhavna thought about the hub: targets on every wall, a scoreboard of late deliveries, Kunal's name at the top of the shift chart. At dinner she said, lightly, "You weren't you today. At home you'd never talk to anyone like that. Is the job doing that?" Kunal put his fork down. "Was it that bad?"

"Raghav, can I ask you something without you getting upset?" Vidya passed him the rotis.
"That's never a good start, Didi."
"I came by the mall today to drop your lunchbox. I saw you at the security desk."
"And?"
"You made that cleaning lady open her whole bag in front of everyone. Then you said, 'People like you always try something.'"
Raghav's jaw tightened. "It's procedure. We've had thefts."
"Okay. But at home you carry Amma's shopping up four floors without being asked. You'd never talk to her like that."
"It's different there. The manager watches the CCTV. If anything goes missing, it's on me."
"I believe you. That's what I mean: the job's pushing you into someone else. I just didn't recognise my little brother."
Raghav was quiet for a long time. "Her name's Shanthi," he said at last. "She's worked there longer than me."

qa.a: At the security desk.

qa.a: It suggests Raghav is beginning to see Shanthi as a person again and feels uneasy about how he treated her.

qa.a: Vidya asked first, believed him about the pressure, and blamed the job for pushing him rather than calling him cruel, so he could think instead of defend.

qa.q: What might it be like for Shanthi to open her bag in front of everyone?
qa.a: Shanthi, who has worked there longer than Raghav, would likely feel humiliated and treated as a suspect rather than a colleague.

passage: I'm Sarita. Last spring my college friend Kartik became a shift supervisor at the call centre where I also work. Kartik is the person who remembers everyone's birthday and cries at weddings. So it took me a while to believe what I saw: him standing behind Himani, a new trainee, reading her call transcript aloud to the floor and saying, 'This is what not to do.' She kept her eyes on her keyboard. I was angry. My first thought was to post about it in our friends' chat. Instead I thought about the floor: the live scoreboard, the managers upstairs listening in, the way everyone there talks faster and colder. It wasn't an excuse, but it explained something. Over chai I said, 'Kartik, that's not how you are at home. I think this place is getting into you.' He was defensive for a minute, then asked, 'What would you have done?'

qa.q: What did Kartik read aloud to the floor?
qa.a: Himani's call transcript, saying, 'This is what not to do.'

qa.q: What did Sarita feel at first, and what changed Sarita's mind?
qa.a: Sarita was angry and wanted to post in the friends' chat, but thinking about the scoreboard and managers listening in helped Sarita see how the place was shaping Kartik.

qa.q: Which choice did Sarita make instead of posting, and what did it open up?
qa.a: Sarita talked to Kartik over chai, naming the change and the place, which moved Kartik from defensive to asking what Sarita would have done.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Himani?
qa.a: Himani, a new trainee, was humiliated in front of the whole floor and could only keep her eyes on her keyboard 😔

Note, 9 December. Written by Sangeeta, senior teacher, residential school.

Mohan, twenty-five, took over as boys' hostel warden this term. We have been friends since training college. At home he makes paper boats for his nieces and lets them win at ludo. Tonight I saw him make three Class 6 boys stand outside the dormitory in the cold for talking after lights-out. When one, Gopika's younger brother, started to cry, Mohan said, "Crying won't help you." That is not the Mohan I know.

I also know the job: sixty boys, no deputy, a principal who blames the warden for every complaint.

What I did next: I brought the boys inside, then waited until he was calmer. I said, "This isn't how you are at home. I think the job is pushing you somewhere you wouldn't go." He was silent, then asked if I'd help him draft fair rules and raise the need for a deputy with the principal.

qa.q: How many boys does Mohan look after as warden?
qa.a: He looks after sixty boys.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she saw Mohan with the boys outside the dormitory?
qa.a: Sangeeta was troubled and surprised, since the harsh warden in front of Sangeeta was not the gentle friend who plays ludo with his nieces.

qa.q: Which part of Sangeeta's approach helped Mohan listen?
qa.a: Waiting until he was calmer and linking his behaviour to the pressures of the job, rather than attacking him, let him admit it and ask for help.

qa.q: What was that cold night like for the three Class 6 boys?
qa.a: They were left outside in the cold and told crying would not help, which likely made them feel scared and unprotected by the person meant to care for them.

grounding: A teacher sees a friend become harsh in his warden role, notes it is not how he is at home, and raises it gently while recognising the job's pressures.

passage:
Friday night

Saw Deven at work today for the first time. He's a ticket checker on the metro now. A college boy didn't have a valid card, and Deven held him by the elbow in front of the whole platform and said, "People like you think rules are for others." The boy was shaking. Deven's voice was one I'd never heard.

This is the Deven who used to cry at the end of films. Who carries his grandmother's shopping bags without being asked.

My first thought was to message Jasleen, his sister, and say, "Your brother has become a bully." I didn't. I thought about his job: the fines targets, the cameras everywhere, the supervisors listening on radios.

Tonight I called him. I said, "Deven, today on the platform that wasn't you. At home you'd never talk like that. I think the uniform's doing something." Long pause. Then: "I didn't even notice."

- Alka

qa.q: What is Deven's job now?
qa.a: He is a ticket checker on the metro.

qa.q: Why did Alka decide not to message Jasleen?
qa.a: Alka felt unsure it was fair to blame Deven without thinking about the fines targets, cameras and supervisors that shape his job, so Alka chose to speak to him directly.

qa.q: What did Alka do well when she called Deven?
qa.a: Alka named the behaviour plainly, reminded him of how he is at home, and linked it to the role, so he could hear it without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might the college boy remember the moment on the platform?
qa.a: He would probably remember feeling shamed and frightened in public, as if he were a criminal rather than someone without a valid card.

grounding: Alka sees Deven turn harsh in his ticket-checker role, remarks it is not how he is at home, and raises it without hostility.
